titleText.es: Si pensáis que esto es muy duro con la crítica literaria, leed el artículo de la Wikipedia sobre la deconstrucción.
titleText.en: If you think this is too hard on literary criticism, read the Wikipedia article on deconstruction.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely translates the official English title text and uses the informal plural forms pensáis and leed that are common in Spain.

regions.labelEs: MI HOBBY: SENTARME CON ESTUDIANTES DE POSGRADO Y CONTAR CUÁNTO TARDAN EN DARSE CUENTA DE QUE NO SOY UN EXPERTO EN SU MATERIA.

applications.explanationEn: Me is attached to the unchanged action sentar and identifies the speaker as the person who will sit down.
Sentarme carries the matching me for the person who sits, and con introduces the students who join that action.
Cuánto keeps its accent because it introduces an embedded question about the amount of time.
Tardan gives the time-taking verb, en introduces the action, and darse cuenta supplies the realization action whose duration is measured.
Darse and cuenta form the realization expression, while de que opens the fact that becomes clear.

applications.exampleEs: SOY UN EXPERTO EN SU MATERIA
applications.explanationEn: Soy supplies the form of ser, experto names the claimed level of knowledge, en introduces the field, and su materia supplies that field.

regions.labelEs: NUESTRO GRAN PROBLEMA ES LA DISIPACIÓN DE CALOR.

applications.explanationEn: Habéis is the informal-plural helper and probado is probar's completed-action form.
Habéis is the present-perfect helper used for informal plural “you,” a form especially common in Spain.
Probado gives the attempted action, con introduces the proposed option, and logaritmos fills that option slot.

excludedUnits.rationale: 48 is the measured number of seconds rather than a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: ENTONCES ¿LA FAMILIA UGROFINESA ESTA INCLUYE, POR EJEMPLO, AL KLINGON?

excludedUnits.rationale: KLINGON is the unchanged proper name of a fictional constructed language, not Spanish vocabulary; the linked concept explains why it is the joke's category error.

applications.explanationEn: Familia names the category first, and ugrofinesa follows as its neutral descriptive classification.
Ugrofinesa uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun familia.
Por and ejemplo form the conventional expression that introduces one illustrative member of a category.

excludedUnits.rationale: 63 is the measured number of seconds rather than a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, MI ÚLTIMO TRABAJO CONSISTE EN CLASIFICAR A LA GENTE DE LA MEJOR A LA PEOR.

applications.explanationEn: Consiste introduces the definition, en links it to the activity, and clasificar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
A marks the people as the direct affected target, while la gente names that human group.

applications.exampleEs: DE LA MEJOR A LA PEOR
applications.explanationEn: De introduces the best-ranked endpoint and a introduces the worst-ranked endpoint; each adjective keeps its feminine article because it stands for a feminine person in the group.

excludedUnits.rationale: 4 is the measured number of minutes rather than a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Crítica names the field first, and literaria follows to classify it by its subject matter.
Literaria uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun crítica.

regions.labelEs: VERÁS, LA DECONSTRUCCIÓN ES INEXTRICABLE NO SOLO DEL TEXTO, SINO DEL SER.

applications.exampleEs: NO SOLO DEL TEXTO, SINO DEL SER
applications.explanationEn: No solo marks del texto as the first parallel item, and sino adds the matching second item del ser.

regions.labelEs: OCHO PAPERS Y DOS LIBROS Y TODAVÍA NO SE HAN PERCATADO.

applications.explanationEn: Todavía keeps the situation open up to the current point, and no makes the expected realization remain absent.
Han is the plural present-perfect helper and percatado is percatarse's completed-action form; the preceding se supplies the matching marker for that verb.

cards.noteEn: Hobby is an English loanword used in Spanish. A common Spanish alternative is afición or pasatiempo.

cards.promptEs: hobby · falso experto · disciplinas · segundos y minutos
cards.answerEn: the speaker tests how long graduate students in different fields take to notice that he is bluffing
cards.noteEn: Each panel gives an obviously ill-informed contribution and records the detection time. The literary-criticism group remains unconvinced only after eight papers and two books, which is the final escalation of the joke.

cards.answerEn: to sit down; to sit myself down
cards.noteEn: Sentar means “to seat.” With the matching small word me attached, sentarme normally means that the speaker sits down. The attached me does not need a separate English word.

example.en: I am going to sit down here.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone sits down with another person or group?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of sentarse, then con before the person or group.
cards.noteEn: The short word matches the person who sits: me, te, se, nos, or os. With a changed present-time verb, it comes before: me siento, te sientas, se sienta. With the unchanged dictionary form, attach it: sentarme, sentarte, sentarse, sentarnos, or sentaros. Con stays unchanged and introduces the companion or group.

example.es: Hoy me siento con Ana durante el almuerzo.
example.en: Today I sit down with Ana during lunch.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”
A posgrado is advanced study pursued after completing an initial university degree.

example.en: She is doing graduate studies in history.

cards.answerEn: to time; to count how long
cards.noteEn: Contar often means “to count” or “to tell.” When it is followed by cuánto tardar, it can mean measuring or timing how long something takes.

example.es: La profesora va a contar cuánto tardan en ordenar las tarjetas.
example.en: The teacher is going to time how long they take to sort the cards.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.promptEs: tardar + tiempo + en + acción en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say how long someone takes to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tardar, optionally give the amount of time, then en and the action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The action form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and can carry an attached pronoun: tardaron una hora en llegar; tardan mucho en darse cuenta. Use cuánto to ask the amount of time.

example.en: They took two hours to arrive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links the time taken to the action
to realize; to notice (as part of darse cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Darse combines the dictionary form dar with se attached. It does not mean ‘to give oneself’ here: darse cuenta is the complete fixed expression for realizing or noticing something.

example.es: Marta puede darse cuenta del error.

cards.promptEs: darse cuenta de (que) + hecho o situación
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone realizes or becomes aware of something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun, a form of dar, cuenta, and then de before what is realized.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun and dar must match the person: me doy cuenta, te das cuenta, se da cuenta, nos damos cuenta, and so on. Use de before a noun and de que before a full statement. Cuenta is not translated separately in this expression.

example.es: Nos dimos cuenta de que faltaba una llave.
example.en: We realized that a key was missing.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes darse cuenta, “to realize”
cards.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account, bill, or calculation. In darse cuenta, it is part of a fixed expression and is not translated separately.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta muy tarde.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces what is realized after darse cuenta
cards.noteEn: After darse cuenta, de introduces the fact or thing that becomes clear. Before a full statement, Spanish normally uses de que.

example.es: Se dio cuenta de que era tarde.
example.en: She realized that it was late.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is an expert in a subject or field?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ser, experto or experta, and en before the field.
cards.noteEn: Experto changes to match the person: experto, experta, expertos, or expertas. The field can be a noun or an action used as a noun.

example.en: Ana is an expert in linguistics.

cards.noteEn: Su stays singular because the possessed thing is singular, even when the owners are several people. Sus is used before a plural possessed thing.
Materia can mean physical matter, but in education it means a subject or area of knowledge.

example.es: La física es su materia favorita.

cards.noteEn: Grande shortens to gran directly before a singular noun. Here it describes importance or significance rather than physical size.
In engineering, disipación describes unwanted energy, especially heat, being spread out and removed from a system.

example.es: El ventilador mejora la disipación de calor.

cards.noteEn: Calor is masculine in standard Spanish: el calor. It can refer to thermal energy or the feeling of being hot.

cards.answerEn: you all have (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Habéis is the present helper form of haber used with vosotros or vosotras. It comes before a completed-action form such as llegado or oído.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?
How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.noteEn: Probado is probar's completed-action form. After a form of haber, it asks or states whether an option has been tried.

example.en: Have you all tried another solution?

cards.promptEs: probar con + persona, cosa u opción
cards.questionEn: How do you say that you will try a particular person, thing, or option to see whether it works?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of probar, then con, then the person, thing, or option being tried.
cards.noteEn: Probar by itself can mean to try, test, or taste. Con introduces the chosen possibility in this pattern. Only probar changes for the person and time; con stays unchanged.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces the person, thing, or option tried after probar
cards.noteEn: In probar con, con marks the chosen possibility that someone will try to see whether it works. English normally says “try” directly before that option, without a separate word for con.
A logarithm answers what exponent is needed to produce a given number from a chosen base.
Lingüística is the systematic study of language and how languages work.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: Klingon is a constructed fictional language from Star Trek, not a member of the Finno-Ugric language family
cards.noteEn: The Finno-Ugric branch includes real languages such as Finnish, Estonian, and Hungarian. Suggesting Klingon as another member exposes that the speaker is bluffing about linguistics.
Ugrofinesa describes the branch of the Uralic language family that includes Finnish, Estonian, and Hungarian. It uses feminine singular -a to match familia.

example.es: El finés es una lengua ugrofinesa.

cards.noteEn: Incluye is the present form of incluir used with one person, thing, group, or category.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por ejemplo (“for example”)

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce an example?
cards.noteEn: Por ejemplo works like English “for example” or “for instance.” It can introduce an example before or after a complete statement.

example.es: Me gustan muchos deportes, por ejemplo, el tenis.
example.en: I like many sports—for example, tennis.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; a + el before the named language
cards.noteEn: The printed al combines a and el before the specifically named language. Natural English simply names the language after “include.”

example.es: El grupo incluye al dialecto local.
example.en: The group includes the local dialect.

cards.noteEn: Sociología is the study of societies, social relationships, and institutions.

example.en: She studies sociology at the university.

cards.noteEn: Before a noun, último can mean the final or last remaining one, or simply the most recent one. The surrounding noun and situation distinguish those readings: el último superviviente is the last survivor, while mi último trabajo can mean my latest work.
Consiste is a present form of consistir. Spanish normally follows it with en before the defining activity or components.

example.es: El trabajo consiste en comparar datos.
example.en: The work consists of comparing data.

cards.promptEs: consistir en + acción en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say what an activity or process consists of doing?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of consistir, then en and the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged action form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir: consiste en comparar, aprender, or decidir. English normally says “consists of doing.”

example.es: La tarea consiste en comparar dos textos.
example.en: The task consists of comparing two texts.

cards.answerEn: of; introduces what something consists of
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses consistir en before the activity or components. English normally uses “consist of.”

example.es: La prueba consiste en ordenar las piezas.
example.en: The test consists of arranging the pieces.

cards.noteEn: Clasificar can mean placing things in categories or arranging them by a ranking.

example.es: Van a clasificar los resultados de mejor a peor.
example.en: They are going to rank the results from best to worst.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: from; marks the start of a range
cards.noteEn: In the paired pattern de ... a ..., de introduces the starting point and a introduces the endpoint.

example.es: Ordena las notas de la mejor a la peor.
example.en: Order the grades from best to worst.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a range from one endpoint to another?
cards.answerEn: Put de before the starting point and a before the endpoint.
cards.noteEn: Articles and other determiners stay with each endpoint: de la mejor a la peor; del lunes al viernes. The same frame works for rankings, places, and times.

example.en: She works from Monday to Friday.

cards.noteEn: With el, la, lo, los, or las, mejor usually means “best.” Without one of those words, it often means “better.”

cards.answerEn: to; marks the end of a range
cards.noteEn: In the paired pattern de ... a ..., de introduces the starting point and a introduces the endpoint.

example.es: Ordena las notas de la mejor a la peor.
example.en: Order the grades from best to worst.

cards.noteEn: With el, la, los, or las, peor normally means “worst.” Without an article it often means “worse.”
Crítica can name the activity or field of analyzing and evaluating art, literature, or ideas.

cards.answerEn: deconstruction is a literary and philosophical approach that examines unstable meanings and oppositions within texts
cards.noteEn: The panel imitates dense theoretical language by claiming that deconstruction cannot be separated from either the text or the self. The title text extends the joke by pointing readers to a difficult encyclopedia article on the topic.
Literaria describes something related to literature and uses feminine singular -a with a noun such as crítica.
Verás literally has the future form ‘you will see.’ In conversation it can instead introduce a clarification, much like English ‘you see.’

example.en: You see, the plan has changed.

cards.noteEn: In literary theory, deconstrucción is an approach that examines tensions, assumptions, and unstable contrasts within a text.

example.es: El ensayo aplica la deconstrucción al texto.
example.en: The essay applies deconstruction to the text.

cards.noteEn: Inextricable describes things connected so tightly that they cannot be separated or untangled.
No combines with solo to introduce the first part of the paired contrast no solo ... sino ....

example.es: No solo llamó, sino que vino.
example.en: She not only called, but also came.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “not only X, but also Y”?
cards.answerEn: Use no solo before the first matching item and sino before the second.
cards.noteEn: Keep the two sides grammatically parallel. Before a full changed verb, use sino que: no solo llamó, sino que vino. También may be added after sino, but it is not required.

example.es: No solo estudia física, sino química.
example.en: She studies not only physics, but also chemistry.

cards.noteEn: After no, solo marks the first item in a contrast that later adds another item with sino.

example.es: No solo llamó, sino que vino.
example.en: She not only called, but also came.

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.answerEn: but also; introduces the added contrast after no solo
cards.noteEn: Sino introduces the second noun, description, or matching phrase after no solo. Before a full changed verb, Spanish commonly uses sino que.

example.es: No solo estudia física, sino química.
example.en: She studies not only physics, but also chemistry.

cards.noteEn: Ser usually appears as the dictionary form “to be.” With an article, el ser can instead be a noun meaning a being, existence, or the self.

example.es: El ensayo reflexiona sobre el ser.

cards.answerEn: academic papers; research articles (informal English borrowing)
cards.noteEn: Spanish often prefers artículos or trabajos académicos. In academic conversation, the English borrowing paper is also used informally; its plural is papers.

example.en: She published two academic papers on astronomy.

cards.noteEn: Libros is the masculine plural of libro.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use todavía no before the action, or alone when the action is understood.
cards.noteEn: The Spanish order literally resembles “still not,” while natural English often uses “not yet.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks percatarse, “to notice”
cards.noteEn: Percatarse uses a matching small word: me, te, se, nos, or os. Se is used with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.
Percatado is percatarse's completed-action form. With se and a form of haber, it says that someone has noticed or realized something.

example.es: Los técnicos se han percatado del error.
example.en: The technicians have noticed the error.
